strengths: The core dataset contribution is substantial and relevant: SELVABOX contains 83,137 manually annotated tropical tree crowns over 510.6 ha, three countries, multiple forest types, four drones, and 1.2–5.1 cm/px imagery. This meaningfully expands scarce open tropical-forest resources.
The paper addresses a practically important environmental-monitoring problem and clearly motivates why RGB UAV imagery and individual-crown detection matter.

The evaluation is broad: it compares CNN and transformer detectors, multiple resolutions and physical extents, single- and multi-resolution training, raster-level aggregation, and transfer across several tropical, temperate, and urban datasets.

The authors report standard COCO metrics in addition to the proposed raster-level metric, use repeated runs with error bars for their models, and provide extensive hyperparameter, preprocessing, split, and qualitative-result appendices.

The results contain concrete positive evidence: DINO-Swin-L trained only on SELVABOX performs strongly on the held-out BCI50ha tropical dataset, while joint training is competitive across a diverse collection of datasets.
The proposed spatial AOIs, preprocessing and aggregation tools, released data, code, pretrained weights, and permissive licenses could make the work useful beyond the paper itself.
The limitations section acknowledges single-pass annotations and potential misuse for locating valuable trees.
weaknesses: Annotation quality is insufficiently validated for a dataset paper. Most crowns receive only a single annotation pass; there is no independent audit, inter-annotator agreement, measured omission rate, or quantitative analysis of label uncertainty, despite the acknowledged difficulty and incompleteness of crown labeling. Manually selecting especially complete, artifact-free test AOIs further makes the benchmark less representative of deployment conditions.

The central zero-shot claim is overstated. NMS and confidence thresholds are selected using Detectree2 validation labels, so evaluation on Detectree2 is not strictly target-label-free zero-shot transfer. The paper also could not recover Detectree2's original splits and explicitly admits possible leakage for the published Detectree2 baselines, making that comparison unreliable.

The benefit attributed to the multi-resolution method is not cleanly established. On SELVABOX it mainly preserves, rather than improves, accuracy, and the paper does not provide the key fixed-resolution-versus-multi-resolution ablation on external OOD datasets. Thus the claimed OOD benefit is confounded with the larger DINO/Swin-L architecture, training recipe, and training-data composition.

Claims about the value of SELVABOX are partly confounded by unequal model capacity and data scale. Stronger controls would train the same architecture and recipe on each source dataset, match annotation counts or geographic area, and report leave-one-dataset-out experiments. Adding SELVABOX to N+Q+O barely changes non-tropical performance and sometimes slightly lowers it.

The proposed RF175 metric is weakly justified: the 0.75 IoU threshold is chosen heuristically, no sensitivity analysis is provided, and there is no empirical validation that RF175 better tracks downstream counting or biomass objectives. Optimizing both score and NMS thresholds also creates considerable validation-set selection flexibility.

The split protocol reduces but may not eliminate spatial leakage: several AOIs are immediately adjacent within the same orthomosaic, with no stated geographic buffer or distance-based sensitivity analysis. Moreover, removal of zero-annotation tiles appears to be applied during external-dataset preprocessing, which can undermeasure false positives and bias evaluation.

Reproducibility reporting remains incomplete despite the released-resource claims: the manuscript does not state the number or identities of random seeds underlying the error bars, leaves many settings at framework defaults, and reports an approximate hyperparameter search without fully specifying its candidate space.
The ethical discussion offers no concrete mitigation for the acknowledged risk that georeferenced imagery and predictions could facilitate targeted illegal logging.

strengths: SELVABOX is a potentially valuable resource: 83,137 manually annotated crowns from high-resolution UAV imagery across 14 orthomosaics in Brazil, Ecuador, and Panama.

The paper addresses an important, underrepresented application with clear ecological relevance, and the inclusion of data, preprocessing tools, training code, pretrained weights, and permissive licenses supports reuse.

The experiments cover multiple architectures, resolutions, spatial extents, and external datasets. Reporting results over multiple seeds and providing extensive implementation details are positive reproducibility practices.
Spatially defined splits and raster-level aggregation are motivated by genuine shortcomings of conventional randomly tiled evaluation.
weaknesses: Annotation reliability is insufficiently established for a dataset paper. Most labels received only a single annotation pass, no inter-annotator agreement or expert audit is reported, crown inclusion is subjective, and several rasters are acknowledged to contain incomplete annotations. Manually masking visibly sparse regions does not quantify or resolve residual missing-label bias.

The evaluation appears to remove zero-annotation tiles, including during preprocessing of evaluation datasets. This uses ground-truth knowledge to select evaluated imagery, can suppress false positives in crown-free or unlabeled regions, and undermines the claim that RF1_75 measures operational performance over complete rasters.

The proposed splits are not convincing geographic generalization tests. Training, validation, and test regions can be directly adjacent within the same orthomosaic, without a stated spatial buffer. Consequently, near-duplicate local appearance, acquisition conditions, and strong spatial autocorrelation may remain across splits.

RF1_75 is weakly validated. The choice of IoU 0.75 is heuristic, potentially brittle under noisy single-pass boxes, and arguably poorly aligned with the stated counting motivation. Its score is also strongly affected by NMS and confidence thresholds selected through a relatively large grid. Sensitivity analyses across IoU thresholds, aggregation procedures, and complete-raster coverage are missing.

The broad state-of-the-art and generalization claims exceed the evidence. Tropical OOD evaluation uses only two datasets; on Detectree2, the authors explicitly cannot reproduce the original split and acknowledge possible train-test leakage in the principal competing method. This makes that comparison unsuitable as strong SOTA evidence.

The multi-dataset experiment does not isolate the contribution of SELVABOX from added annotation volume, geographic diversity, and training distribution. Size-matched sampling, per-country leave-one-region-out tests, and controlled dataset-addition ablations are absent.

Methodological novelty is limited: the detector is an existing DINO/Swin-L model, while the multi-resolution method is standard random cropping and resizing. Comparisons omit several newer detection architectures despite claiming an exhaustive benchmark.

The dataset covers only a small number of acquisition sites and drone surveys, so the annotation count overstates its independent environmental diversity. Stronger cross-site, cross-country, seasonal, and sensor-held-out evaluation would be needed to substantiate broad tropical-forest generalization.

Overall, the resource has promise, but weaknesses in label quality assurance and potentially ground-truth-dependent evaluation are central for a benchmark contribution. These issues make the current evidence insufficient for acceptance at a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: SELVABOX is a significant resource contribution: 83,137 manually annotated crowns across 510.1 hectares, three tropical countries, multiple forest types, four drones, and resolutions from 1.2–5.1 cm/px. Its scale substantially exceeds prior open tropical crown datasets.
The paper addresses an important, societally relevant problem for which representative tropical data are genuinely scarce.

The evaluation is unusually broad for a dataset paper, covering CNN and transformer detectors, resolution and spatial-extent ablations, multi-resolution training, raster-level aggregation, and transfer across five external datasets.

The spatially separated splits, explicit masking of incompletely annotated regions, raster-level RF1 metric, repeated runs with uncertainty estimates, and detailed preprocessing and hyperparameter appendices demonstrate careful experimental practice.

The released dataset, preprocessing and benchmarking libraries, pretrained weights, standardized external-dataset conversions, and permissive licenses provide strong practical and reproducibility value.

Results provide concrete evidence of utility: SELVABOX-trained models substantially improve zero-shot performance on BCI50ha, while joint training remains competitive across tropical, temperate, and urban benchmarks.
weaknesses: Annotation quality assurance is the main concern for a dataset contribution. Most crowns received only a single annotation pass, and the paper reports neither inter-annotator agreement nor an expert audit of a representative subset. This leaves the consistency of boxes produced by six annotators insufficiently quantified.

The test regions were deliberately selected for dense annotations, minimal reconstruction artifacts, and high visual quality. Although understandable, this makes the benchmark less representative of operational deployment and may overestimate performance on typical imagery.

Some claimed out-of-distribution results are not strictly target-agnostic: Detectree2 validation data are used to select NMS and confidence thresholds before evaluation on its test set. These results should be distinguished from the genuinely zero-shot BCI50ha evaluation.

The central multi-resolution method is a relatively simple crop-and-resize augmentation, and its in-domain gains are mostly within standard deviation. The paper's strongest novelty therefore lies in the dataset and benchmark rather than methodology.

The architecture comparisons do not fully isolate the source of improvement: the strongest DINO model also uses a much larger Swin-L backbone, and comparisons against more recent detection architectures or parameter-matched alternatives are limited.

The state-of-the-art framing is somewhat stronger than the evidence warrants because several competing methods are older domain-specific systems, the original Detectree2 split could not be reconstructed, and dataset-specific preprocessing and annotation conventions complicate direct comparisons.

Multi-dataset training would be easier to interpret with clearer reporting or ablations for dataset sampling balance, per-dataset contribution, computational cost, and whether improvements arise primarily from SELVABOX scale or from resolution augmentation.

strengths: SELVABOX is a substantial and potentially valuable resource: 83,137 expert-produced crown annotations across 14 high-resolution orthomosaics, three tropical countries, multiple forest types, sensors, and ground resolutions.
The paper addresses an important, underrepresented application and makes a credible case that existing open tropical tree-crown datasets are too small for robust model development.

The evaluation is unusually extensive for a dataset paper, covering CNN and transformer detectors, multiple resolutions and spatial extents, multi-resolution training, three random seeds, standard COCO metrics, raster-level evaluation, and transfer across several external datasets.

The results provide concrete evidence of the dataset's utility. Models trained only on SELVABOX generalize strongly to BCI50ha, while joint training produces competitive results across tropical, temperate, and urban datasets.

Spatially defined splits, detailed preprocessing and hyperparameter documentation, released code, pretrained weights, standardized external-dataset conversions, and permissive licensing substantially strengthen reproducibility and practical impact.
The paper discusses annotation incompleteness, responsible use, and limitations of remotely interpreted labels rather than presenting the resource as error-free.
weaknesses: Annotation quality is not quantitatively established. There is no inter-annotator agreement study, independent audit sample, estimate of missed-crown frequency, or comparison against field or LiDAR references. Qualitative expert review alone is insufficient to characterize label uncertainty in highly ambiguous, overlapping canopies.

The split design may overestimate generalization within SELVABOX. Train, validation, and test regions are sometimes adjacent portions of the same orthomosaic, with no reported spatial buffer or distance analysis, while test regions were deliberately selected for annotation completeness and minimal reconstruction artifacts. This creates residual spatial-correlation and test-selection concerns.

Several state-of-the-art claims conflate the effects of dataset scale, architecture, training data, augmentation, and compute. The strongest method uses a large DINO/Swin-L detector, whereas prominent external methods use older architectures and released default inference configurations. Adding SELVABOX also increases the amount of training data and optimization exposure; matched-budget or size-controlled experiments are absent.

RF1 at IoU 0.75 is useful operationally but remains an author-selected metric whose score depends strongly on validation-tuned confidence and NMS thresholds. The rationale for exactly 0.75 is largely qualitative, and the metric is unavailable for some datasets, complicating uniform comparisons. Standard mAP/mAR reporting mitigates but does not eliminate this concern.

The claimed zero-shot status on Detectree2 is difficult to interpret because the original splits could not be recovered, and the authors' evaluation regions may overlap data used to train the released Detectree2 models. Results on this benchmark should not support broad comparative claims.

The crown-size distribution tests add limited evidence: statistical significance is nearly guaranteed at these sample sizes, spatially correlated crowns are treated as independent observations, and differences in bounding-box size do not establish broader morphological or ecological diversity.

Bounding boxes derived from RGB photo-interpretation capture visible crown-like regions rather than verified individual trees. The paper occasionally describes the task as crown 'delineation' and connects it to counting or biomass estimation more strongly than the provided validation supports.

strengths: SELVABOX is a potentially valuable open resource: 83,137 expert-produced crown boxes across 14 high-resolution orthomosaics, three tropical countries, multiple forest types, drones, and ground sampling distances. Its scale substantially exceeds prior manually annotated tropical datasets.

The paper documents acquisition, preprocessing, spatial splits, masking, augmentation, training, and inference in considerable detail, and promises public data, code, pretrained weights, raster annotations, and standardized versions of external datasets.

The empirical study is broad, covering multiple detector families, resolutions, spatial extents, three seeds for newly trained models, raster-level aggregation, and evaluation across several tropical and non-tropical datasets.
The results provide useful evidence that DINO with a Swin-L backbone is substantially stronger than the CNN alternatives considered, and that SELVABOX training transfers well to BCI50ha.
The authors explicitly discuss incomplete annotations, dataset limitations, ecological misuse, and the need to treat model outputs as decision support rather than definitive measurements.
weaknesses: The dataset's central quality claim is insufficiently validated. There is no quantitative inter-annotator agreement, independent reannotation study, estimate of missed-tree frequency, or comparison with field/LiDAR-derived ground truth. Ambiguous intertwined crowns and manually selected masking regions are handled procedurally but not measured, despite label completeness being crucial for detection metrics.

The proposed train/validation/test splits often occupy adjacent regions of the same orthomosaic and acquisition. Preventing pixel overlap does not eliminate spatial, ecological, or sensor-level autocorrelation. Results on this split may therefore overstate generalization; a stronger evaluation would hold out complete sites, flights, or orthomosaics.

The claimed zero-shot protocol is not consistently strict. Detectree2 labels are used to tune NMS and confidence thresholds, so performance there is not fully label-free. Its original splits could not be recovered, and the paper itself acknowledges possible train-test leakage, yet still makes state-of-the-art claims on this benchmark.

Several headline conclusions are confounded. Comparisons combine changes in training data, architecture, backbone capacity, input size, augmentation, and hyperparameter tuning. In particular, there is no controlled cross-dataset comparison of single-resolution versus multi-resolution training, so the claim that the proposed augmentation drives OOD generalization is not established.

Baseline fairness is questionable: the authors' models receive extensive per-setting hyperparameter searches and larger inputs, whereas released competitors are evaluated largely with their existing/default pipelines. Dataset-specific annotation conventions also differ, complicating direct ranking. Claims of matching or exceeding competing methods should consequently be more qualified.

RF1 at a single IoU threshold is essentially raster-level F1 after NMS rather than a substantial new metric. The choice of IoU=0.75 is justified only heuristically, and exhaustive validation-set tuning of confidence and NMS thresholds can favor this metric. Re-optimizing postprocessing separately at every IoU also produces non-monotonic curves and weakens the claimed threshold-robust interpretation.

The paper sometimes overstates the evidence: SELVABOX-only transfer is poor on Detectree2, the multi-dataset model remains below Detectree2-resize in the principal RF1 metric there, and adding SELVABOX yields negligible or mixed changes on the non-tropical datasets. Thus the broad claim of state-of-the-art generalization across tropical and non-tropical settings is not uniformly supported.

The methodological novelty beyond the dataset is limited: random crop-and-resize augmentation, standard detectors, NMS aggregation, and F1 evaluation are straightforward. Given the unresolved annotation-quality and evaluation-design issues, the otherwise substantial resource falls slightly below the acceptance threshold for a top-tier AI conference.

The experimental study is unusually broad for a dataset paper, covering multiple architectures, spatial resolutions, tile extents, training-dataset combinations, and six evaluation datasets.

The spatially separated splits, masking of known incompletely annotated regions, three-seed results for newly trained models, and disclosure of preprocessing, training, and inference hyperparameters demonstrate considerable methodological care.

The multi-resolution pipeline is simple and practically useful: one model remains competitive across several resolutions, while models trained with SELVABOX show substantial gains on the held-out BCI50ha benchmark.
The promised release of annotations, standardized external datasets, code, pretrained weights, and two reusable libraries gives the work strong practical value and reproducibility potential.
weaknesses: The central annotation resource lacks quantitative reliability measurements such as inter-annotator agreement, double-annotation statistics, or validation against field or LiDAR data. Expert review is valuable, but the paper's assertion that annotation variability was not significant is unsupported quantitatively.

The in-distribution split is spatially separated but often drawn from adjacent areas of the same orthomosaics, flights, and sites. A site- or orthomosaic-held-out evaluation would provide stronger evidence of geographic generalization and reduce residual spatial and acquisition-condition correlation.

Some claims are overstated. Higher resolution improves mAP fairly consistently, but does not consistently improve RF1_75 for every architecture and configuration. Likewise, the broad state-of-the-art claim rests on a limited set of detector families and comparisons with unequal training-data budgets.

The Detectree2 evaluation is not fully controlled because the original train/test split could not be recovered. Moreover, labeled Detectree2 validation data are used to tune NMS parameters, so describing that dataset evaluation as strictly zero-shot is debatable, even though its images are excluded from model training.

RF1_75 is operationally motivated and threshold ablations are provided, but its weighted average of per-raster F1 scores is nonstandard, the 0.75 choice remains somewhat heuristic, and inference parameters are selected using the best model seed. Reporting global micro-F1 and a threshold-averaged raster metric under a seed-independent tuning protocol would make the conclusions more robust.
